**Date: 2025-11-20**  
Summary: Toyota Motor Corporation announced a two-week production halt for its Camry and RAV4 gasoline models at three North American plants starting November 25, citing persistent chip shortages from Nexperia. The disruption follows the Dutch-controlled chipmaker’s limited export permits under the U.S.-China agreement, which Toyota says cannot meet its Q4 demand. On December 2, 2025, General Motors announced a temporary halt in production of its mid-size gas SUVs at its Arlington, Texas plant, citing intensified supply chain disruptions from the lingering aluminum shortage and new semiconductor allocation constraints. The move follows Ford's prolonged F-150 Lightning pause and escalating tariff-related costs. GM expects the shutdown to reduce fourth-quarter output by 12,000 vehicles, impacting popular models like the Chevrolet Tahoe and GMC Yukon. CEO Mary Barra stated the company is prioritizing higher-margin trucks and EVs amid a "challenging period of geopolitical and material headwinds." Analysts estimate the halt will cost GM $800 million in lost revenue as inventory of mid-size gas vehicles tightens across the U.S. market.

On November 28, 2025, Toyota announced a 12% reduction in its global production forecast for mid-size gas vehicles, citing persistent semiconductor shortages from the Nexperia crisis and higher US tariff costs. The automaker expects to sell 150,000 fewer units in North America and Southeast Asia through Q1 2026. Toyota also delayed the launch of its redesigned Camry by six months as it reallocates chips to higher-margin hybrids. The move follows similar profit warnings from Honda and Ford. Industry analysts note that mid-size gas vehicle margins are under severe pressure from both rising input costs and Chinese EV competition. Toyota's shares fell 3.2% on the announcement.

On December 10, 2025, Ford announced that the F-150 Lightning production halt caused by an aluminum supplier fire will extend until at least mid-2026, costing an additional $1 billion in lost revenue. The company also disclosed that new tariffs on imported steel and aluminum, part of the Trump administration's trade policy, have raised material costs by 12% across its gasoline vehicle lineup. The European Union is expected to propose new subsidies for domestic battery and chip production by year-end, responding to the ongoing supply chain disruptions.

On December 15, 2025, Ford announced that its F-150 Lightning production would remain suspended through at least Q2 2026 due to ongoing repairs at the aluminum supplier's fire-damaged plant. The company revised its 2026 EV production targets downward by 40%, redirecting resources to hybrid F-150 models that saw a 35% sales surge in November. Meanwhile, Volkswagen reported that its Chinese semiconductor replacement effort has identified alternative suppliers for 60% of critical chips, but warned that full decoupling remains three years away. Hyundai and Kia continued to see hybrid growth, with Kia posting a 5% overall sales increase in early December, driven by the Sportage hybrid. The industry’s shift away from full EVs accelerated, as six more states proposed eliminating EV purchase incentives.

Volkswagen announced on December 15, 2025, that it will revive a dedicated mid-size gasoline SUV platform for North America and Europe, responding to flagging EV demand and persistently strong consumer preference for gas-powered family vehicles. The decision follows the automaker's 160-billion-euro investment plan and reverses earlier commitments to go all-electric in those segments by 2030. CEO Oliver Blume cited the end of EV tax credits in the US and slower-than-expected charging infrastructure buildout as key drivers. The first model under the revived platform is expected in early 2027 and will be assembled at VW's Chattanooga plant, leveraging existing supply chains for internal combustion components. The move mirrors strategies from Ford and Hyundai, which reported marginal US sales declines in November after federal EV incentives expired, with hybrid and gas models gaining share.

On 2025-12-12, Ford Motor Company announced a temporary halt in production of its mid-size gas vehicles at two US plants through January 2026, citing a persistent shortage of semiconductor chips and rare earth magnets previously sourced from China. The shutdown affects the Ford Escape and Edge models, which rely heavily on Chinese suppliers for electronic control units and electric steering components. Ford is redirecting available chips to higher-margin EV production. The move follows CEO Jim Farley’s recent warnings on supply chain vulnerability and aligns with industry-wide efforts to reduce dependency on Chinese inputs, as highlighted by German automakers in late November. Analysts expect further production curtailments across the sector as automakers scramble to secure alternative sources.

On December 15, 2025, Ford Motor Company announced plans to expand magnet production in North America, citing the newly secured rare-earth export licenses from China as a bridge to a more diversified supply chain. Ford will partner with a U.S. mining startup to build a processing facility in Texas, aiming to reduce dependence on Chinese rare earths by 2027. The move comes as German automakers, excluded from Beijing's streamlined permits, press Washington for trade concessions. BMW confirmed it is in talks with Canadian rare-earth suppliers, while Volkswagen reiterated that its supply remains stable despite the licensing disparity. Industry analysts warn that the selective export regime could deepen transatlantic tensions as automakers race to secure critical minerals for hybrid and EV production.

On December 22, 2025, Ford Motor Company announced it expects to fully restore production of mid-size gas vehicles by January 2026, following the streamlined export licenses for rare-earth magnets from China. The easing of supply constraints will allow Ford to meet strong demand for its gas-powered models, which have seen a resurgence as EV incentives ended. Meanwhile, Hyundai reported a 12% increase in hybrid sales in December, offsetting a 50% drop in EV sales. The U.S. market continues to favor traditional powertrains amid policy uncertainty. Automakers are adjusting production lines to prioritize gas and hybrid vehicles for the coming year.

On December 19, 2025, BMW Group announced it will temporarily idle four German plants for one week starting January 12, 2026, due to worsening semiconductor shortages. The move follows Honda’s recent production suspensions in Japan and China and reflects ongoing chip constraints despite earlier policy shifts. BMW CEO Oliver Zipse cited insufficient supply of automotive control chips, particularly from Nexperia’s curtailed output. He criticized the exclusion of German automakers from China’s streamlined rare-earth licenses, warning that reliance on single-source magnets and chips poses systemic risks. The suspension is expected to reduce Q1 2026 output by 40,000 vehicles. Separately, the German auto association VDA urged the EU to fast-track domestic chip and rare-earth investments, similar to JPMorgan’s SRI initiative, as political pressure mounts ahead of the 2026 federal budget talks.

On January 18, 2026, Ford Motor Company announced a multi-year agreement with a European semiconductor manufacturer to secure a stable supply of automotive-grade chips for its mid-size gas vehicle production lines, following the earlier warning from CEO Jim Farley about U.S. dependence on foreign chip sources. The deal, valued at $1.7 billion, covers critical control units and is aimed at preventing production halts similar to those affecting Honda in late 2025. Separately, the U.S. Department of Commerce confirmed that China has extended streamlined rare-earth magnet export licenses to additional non-U.S. automakers, including Volkswagen and BMW, easing supply concerns after months of preferential access for Ford. The developments signal gradual stabilization in key supply chains, though automakers remain cautious.

On February 4, 2026, General Motors announced that it will temporarily idle its assembly plant in Oshawa, Ontario for one week starting February 16 due to the ongoing shortage of semiconductor components used in engine control units. The move affects production of the Chevrolet Equinox and GMC Terrain, both mid-size gasoline models. GM cited persistent supply disruptions following the November removal of China’s Nexperia export curbs, which have not yet fully restored chip availability. The company stated it is working with suppliers in Taiwan and Germany to secure alternative sources but warned that industry-wide production could remain constrained through Q1. The announcement comes amid calls from Ontario Premier Doug Ford for federal HST relief to boost auto sales, though no policy changes have been enacted.

On February 25, 2026, General Motors announced it will idle its midsize SUV assembly plant in Arlington, Texas, for two weeks starting March 2, citing persistent semiconductor allocation issues and rising raw material costs for gas-engine components. The move follows Honda’s recent EV-related warnings and comes as the broader industry grapples with U.S. tariffs on imported steel and aluminum, which have increased production costs for traditional vehicles. GM’s decision underscores that mid-size gas vehicle supply chains remain fragile despite earlier efforts to diversify chip sourcing. The company revised its 2026 North American production forecast downward by 5%, noting that dealer inventories of popular gas models are tightening. Analysts expect the shutdown to reduce Q1 output by roughly 15,000 units and may pressure pricing for mid-size gas SUVs in coming months.

On 2026-02-28, Honda Motor Co. announced a strategic realignment of its North American production, delaying the rollout of several all-electric models originally scheduled for 2027 and diverting investment toward hybrid and mid-size gasoline vehicles. The decision cites persistent U.S. tariffs on imported components, slower-than-expected EV adoption, and the need to stabilize profitability after reporting operating losses in its automobile segment. Honda will retool its Marysville, Ohio plant to produce a new gasoline hybrid Accord and maintain production of the CR-V and Civic, anticipating higher demand for affordable mid-size gas vehicles under current trade conditions. The company also secured additional semiconductor supply agreements with Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers to avoid future production stoppages, complementing the diversification efforts announced in January.

On 2026-03-10, Honda Motor Co. announced plans to increase North American production of its Accord and CR-V mid-size gas models, citing sustained demand and ongoing U.S. tariffs on imported vehicles. The company will invest $650 million in its Ohio plants to expand gasoline powertrain lines, while deferring a previously planned dedicated EV assembly line. Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara said the shift reflects "a pragmatic response to slower-than-expected electrification and persistent trade uncertainty." Honda also confirmed that its semiconductor diversification strategy is on track, with direct contracts now in place with a Taiwanese foundry to supply custom chips for its gas vehicle platforms, reducing reliance on China-sourced components. The move aims to buffer against future supply shocks and maintain profitability in its core mid-size segment.

On March 12, 2026, Toyota Motor North America announced a $1.2 billion investment to upgrade its Georgetown, Kentucky plant for production of a next-generation mid-size gas sedan and SUV, citing steady demand for traditional powertrains amid tariff uncertainty and slower EV adoption. The move reverses earlier EV-centric plans and aligns with Honda's similar reassessment. Toyota plans to launch the refreshed models in early 2027, featuring improved fuel efficiency and hybrid options. The announcement follows Ford’s admission of EV missteps and signals a broader industry pivot to maintain gas vehicle production until charging infrastructure and battery costs improve. Toyota expects the new models to offset declining EV sales in North America and retain market share against Chinese competitors.

The company will delay the launch of its next-generation Honda Prologue EV by 18 months and pause development on a new all-electric Acura model, redirecting funds toward upgrading hybrid gas powertrains for its best-selling CR-V and Accord platforms. Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara stated that current trade policies and charging infrastructure gaps make a pure-EV push unviable in the near term. Honda also disclosed it will sell its stake in a rare-earth processing joint venture in Canada, citing supply chain volatility. The announcement follows a ¥279.5 billion import-duty hit reported in February and intensifies competition from Chinese and Korean automakers offering lower-priced EVs.

The move follows Honda’s recent $15.7 billion EV writedown and pivot to hybrids. Toyota cited consumer preference for affordable, reliable gas vehicles over costly EVs with uncertain resale value. The company will also delay its planned bZ5X EV launch in the U.S. by one year, reallocating investment to upgrade its Georgetown, Kentucky plant for higher gas-model output. Toyota executives emphasized maintaining a flexible product mix, noting that mid-size gas vehicles still account for over 60% of their US sales. The announcement came as Toyota reported steady Q1 gas car sales, contrasting with losses at competitors heavily invested in EVs.

On March 23, 2026, General Motors announced it would delay its next-generation Ultium EV platform by 12–18 months, citing falling demand and uncertainty over federal EV subsidies. CEO Mary Barra said the company would instead redirect capital to hybrid development for North America, following Honda’s lead. GM posted a US$3.2 billion loss in its EV division for Q1 2026, and will idle its Factory Zero Detroit-Hamtramck plant for two months to retool for hybrid production. The decision came after President Trump maintained his stance against EV incentives, pushing more automakers to pivot. Barra acknowledged GM had overcommitted to EVs without adequate policy support, mirroring struggles at Ford and Honda.

On March 19, 2026, Honda announced a strategic pivot to reinvigorate its mid-size gas vehicle lineup in the U.S. and India, aiming to recover from its $15.7 billion writedown and first annual loss in 69 years. The company will boost production of the CR-V and Accord gasoline models in the U.S. and launch two new mid-size sedans with traditional engines in India, targeting stable demand and profitability. CEO Toshihiro Mibe admitted the previous overcommitment to EVs without market readiness and now focuses on gas vehicles to fund a slower, more realistic EV transition. Analysts see this as a necessary but risky move, as Chinese automakers continue aggressive expansion in hybrid and EV segments. Honda also plans to deepen hybrid integration in existing gas models to bridge technology gaps.

On March 24, 2026, Toyota Motor Corporation announced a temporary halt in production of its best-selling mid-size gas sedan models at its Kentucky and Texas plants, citing a shortage of critical electronics components exacerbated by new tariffs on imported steel and aluminum. The halt is expected to reduce Q2 output by 45,000 vehicles. Toyota cited the same supply-chain pressures that forced Ford to cut its free cash flow forecast and follow Honda's pivot to hybrids. Analysts noted that the mid-size gas segment faces mounting inventory costs and weakening demand as U.S. consumers shift to hybrids amid rising fuel prices and policy uncertainty. Toyota shares fell 3% on the news.

On April 1, 2026, Ford Motor Company announced a $6.2 billion writedown of its EV operations in North America and Europe, citing a sharp drop in demand driven by the end of federal EV subsidies under the Trump administration and rising tariff costs on imported battery components. The automaker also confirmed it would indefinitely delay the rollout of three planned fully electric models—a compact SUV, a mid-size truck, and a commercial van—and instead accelerate hybrid production. CEO Jim Farley stated that consumer preference has decisively shifted to hybrids, which now account for 38% of Ford’s U.S. sales. The announcement came as Ford reported a third straight quarterly loss in its EV division, with total EV sales falling 41% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. Analysts warned that Ford’s EV inventory levels are dangerously high, raising the risk of further impairments.

On October 14, 2025, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce officially announced a formal investigation into the Dutch government's invocation of the Goods Availability Act to take control of Nexperia, citing violations of international trade agreements and unfair treatment of Chinese-invested enterprises. Wingtech's legal team filed a comprehensive complaint with the Permanent Court of Arbitration, arguing that the Dutch action constitutes expropriation without due process. Concurrently, China signaled possible retaliatory measures against Dutch semiconductor equipment exports, escalating the dispute. Nexperia's daily operations remain unchanged, but its long-term independence now hinges on diplomatic negotiations, with both sides seeking a resolution before the end of the year.

On October 15, 2025, the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs formally requested that Nexperia suspend certain production lines and halt the transfer of sensitive intellectual property to its Chinese parent, Wingtech, citing national security risks. This directive expands on the earlier September intervention under the Goods Availability Act, specifically targeting chip designs used in automotive and industrial electronics. Nexperia announced it would challenge the order through arbitration, arguing the restrictions exceed Dutch legal authority and unreasonably target commercial operations. Wingtech shares dropped 7% in Hong Kong trading as analysts warned of prolonged operational uncertainty. The European Commission stated it would monitor the case, potentially setting a precedent for national security reviews of foreign-owned semiconductor firms.

On November 20, 2025, Nexperia’s parent Wingtech Technology filed a formal legal challenge at the District Court of The Hague against the Dutch government’s seizure under the Goods Availability Act. Wingtech argues the intervention violates EU investment protections and calls for immediate restoration of operational control. Separately, the US Department of Commerce expanded its Entity List restrictions on Wingtech, tightening export licenses for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The Dutch economic affairs minister stated the government will defend its decision in court, while Nexperia’s interim management confirmed ongoing customer contracts. Industry analysts note the case could set a precedent for foreign investment reviews in critical semiconductor assets across Europe.

On November 6, 2025, the European Commission announced it would launch a formal investigation into the Dutch government's seizure of Nexperia, citing concerns over compliance with EU single-market rules and investment treaty obligations. The Commission’s probe will examine whether the Dutch invocation of the Goods Availability Act constitutes a disproportionate restriction on cross-border corporate governance and property rights. Nexperia’s Chinese parent Wingtech welcomed the investigation, expressing hope for a resolution that restores control and safeguards shareholder value. Meanwhile, the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs defended the intervention as a necessary national security measure, pledging full cooperation with EU authorities. Industry analysts warned that prolonged uncertainty could disrupt supply of specialty chips to European automotive and industrial sectors.

On November 20, 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce announced new export restrictions on gallium and germanium, key inputs for doped electronic materials, directly targeting Nexperia's Dutch operations. The move follows prolonged failure by the Netherlands to resolve the Nexperia seizure dispute. Chinese officials stated the controls are necessary to protect national security and ensure fair treatment of Chinese firms abroad. Nexperia's production of automotive-grade semiconductors faces immediate disruption, as suppliers of these critical raw materials now require special licenses for exports to the Netherlands. Dutch trade authorities condemned the restrictions as retaliatory and counterproductive, while European automakers warned of production halts within weeks. The escalation signals a deepening semiconductor trade conflict with no near-term resolution in sight.

On December 5, 2025, the Dutch and Chinese governments announced a comprehensive agreement to resolve the Nexperia dispute. Under the terms, the Netherlands will fully return control of Nexperia to Wingtech, and China will resume exports of Nexperia's products without restrictions. The agreement includes safeguards for supply chain security and technology independence. Nexperia's former CEO will be reinstated. The Dutch Economy Minister stated that the suspension of state control on November 19 paved the way for this resolution. Automakers and semiconductor industry groups welcomed the deal, noting it alleviates immediate production risks. The dispute had caused shortages of doped electronic materials (HS4 3818) and threatened automotive production since October.

On November 28, 2025, negotiations between the Netherlands and China over Nexperia collapsed after Beijing rejected a Dutch proposal for phased restoration of Wingtech’s control, citing insufficient safeguards for technology transfer. In response, the Dutch government reimposed state control over Nexperia, citing renewed national security risks, and tightened export restrictions on doped electronic materials. Chinese officials retaliated by halting all exports of Nexperia’s finished products, creating an immediate supply shock for automotive semiconductor customers. Automakers reported that production slowdowns resumed, with Toyota and Volkswagen warning of potential plant closures within weeks. The breakdown highlighted escalating geopolitical tensions and the fragility of semiconductor supply chains.

On November 25, 2025, the Dutch government and Chinese officials reached a preliminary agreement on the operational framework for chipmaker Nexperia, according to a joint statement. The deal allows Nexperia’s Chinese unit to continue independent production of doped electronic materials (HS4 3818) for automotive clients, subject to Dutch oversight on technology transfers. Dutch Economy Minister Vincent Karremans described the accord as a “balanced step” to stabilize supply chains, while China’s Ministry of Commerce welcomed the progress. Automakers, including Toyota, reported that chip deliveries for legacy models had normalized, reducing immediate production risks. However, the agreement leaves long-term governance of Nexperia’s intellectual property unresolved, with further talks scheduled for early December.

On December 3, 2025, China and the Netherlands reached a preliminary agreement to stabilize Nexperia's operations, ending a three-month dispute over control of the chipmaker. Under the deal, Nexperia's Chinese unit will resume full exports of finished semiconductors from its Pearl River Delta packaging plant, while the Dutch government formally lifts its September 30 seizure order. Both sides agreed to establish a joint oversight committee to monitor technology transfers and production quotas, addressing national security and supply-chain concerns. The agreement averted a broader automotive chip shortage that had threatened European carmakers reliant on Nexperia's doped electronic materials (HS4 3818). However, industry analysts noted that the resolution left underlying tensions over export controls and Western tech dependence on Chinese manufacturing capacity unresolved.

On December 4, 2025, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce announced new export licensing requirements for doped electronic materials (HS4 3818) produced by Nexperia’s Dongguan facility, citing national security and economic stability. The move effectively restricts shipments of Nexperia China’s output until internal governance disputes with the Dutch headquarters are resolved. The European Commission expressed concern, warning that the standoff could disrupt automotive supply chains across Europe. Nexperia’s Dutch management reiterated its authority over global operations and confirmed it would accelerate the $300 million Malaysia expansion to bypass Chinese production. Wingtech responded by filing a formal complaint with the Dutch courts, demanding restoration of control and an injunction against the Malaysia plan.
